summary: Instructions establish a square bronze-covered altar with utensils and carrying poles, then a rectangular linen-enclosed court with an embroidered gate. The chapter closes by requiring pure olive oil and assigning Aaron and his sons to keep the sanctuary lamp in order from evening to morning.
whyItMatters: The sanctuary plan extends from its inner furnishings to the place of sacrifice and the boundary of its court. Its last verses shift attention from construction to the recurring human work needed to keep worship functioning.

context.author: Exodus does not name its final author. It records Moses writing particular covenant material; traditional Mosaic attribution and modern accounts of composition are distinguished in the book briefing.
context.audience: Israel remembering its rescue from Egypt and its obligations as a covenant community. The chapter does not identify an individual dedicatee.
context.date: The narrative places these events at Sinai after the departure from Egypt. The date of the events and the history of the book’s composition are separate, debated questions.
context.setting: Moses' mountain instruction, describing the outer altar, court, and the priests' future care of the light.
context.literaryForm: Architectural specifications followed by a continuing supply and service requirement.

before.text: The tent's coverings, frame, and inner veil have been described, including the table and lamp stand's positions. The plan now moves to the surrounding working space.

here.text: The altar and enclosure establish the outer arrangement, while the oil command introduces regular priestly responsibility within the tent.

after.text: Aaron and his sons are next named for priestly service, and their garments are specified for their work before God.

outline.heading: The bronze-covered altar
outline.note: A hollow square altar receives horns, utensils, a grating, rings, and carrying poles.

outline.heading: The long sides and west side of the court
outline.note: Linen hangings are supported by pillars and metal fittings.

outline.heading: The eastern gate and overall enclosure
outline.note: A colored entrance screen completes the court, whose dimensions and bronze equipment are summarized.

outline.heading: Oil and the continual light
outline.note: Israel supplies pure oil, and Aaron’s household maintains the lamp from evening to morning.

keyVerses.text: You shall make it hollow with planks. They shall make it as it has been shown you on the mountain.
keyVerses.why: The hollow altar must follow the form shown on the mountain, like the inner furnishings.

keyVerses.text: The length of the court shall be one hundred cubits, and the width fifty throughout, and the height five cubits, of fine twined linen, and their sockets of bronze.
keyVerses.why: The court is described as a bounded space with stated length, width, and height.

keyVerses.text: In the Tent of Meeting, outside the veil which is before the covenant, Aaron and his sons shall keep it in order from evening to morning before Yahweh: it shall be a statute forever throughout their generations on the behalf of the children of Israel.
keyVerses.why: The passage assigns ongoing care of the light to Aaron and his sons for the community.

questions.question: How is the altar shaped and moved?
questions.answer: It is square, five cubits on each side and three high, made hollow with planks and overlaid with bronze. Rings and bronze-covered wooden poles enable carrying, keeping its construction compatible with a movable sanctuary.

questions.question: What are the altar’s “horns”?
questions.answer: They are projections at its four corners, made as one piece with it and covered with bronze. The chapter specifies their position and construction but does not assign a separate symbolic meaning to each projection.

questions.question: What do the utensils reveal about the altar’s use?
questions.answer: Pots for ashes, shovels, basins, meat hooks, and fire pans belong to work involving fire and sacrificial material. The equipment supports the repeated, physical tasks of preparing and tending offerings.

questions.question: What distinguishes the court’s gate?
questions.answer: Its screen uses blue, purple, scarlet, and fine linen embroidery, while the surrounding hangings are fine linen. The east side has two fifteen-cubit stretches flanking the twenty-cubit gateway, which is supported by four pillars.

questions.question: Can the cubit measurements be converted to exact modern units?
questions.answer: The passage measures length, width, and height in cubits without defining a modern conversion. Its stated proportions are clear: a square altar and a court twice as long as it is wide.

questions.question: Who supplies and who tends the light?
questions.answer: The children of Israel bring pure beaten olive oil, while Aaron and his sons keep the lamp in order. The text distributes the work between communal supply and a particular family charged with service.

questions.question: Does “continually” remove the evening-to-morning instruction?
questions.answer: The command speaks of a continual light and then explicitly assigns care from evening to morning before God. Together they describe a continuing obligation with particular attention to nighttime care of the light.

glossary.def: The bronze network fitted beneath the altar’s ledge and associated with its rings.
The silver bands or fittings specified for the court’s pillars.
The pure olive oil required as fuel for the sanctuary light.
